judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 402, which bars public schools from selling, giving out, or serving food on school grounds during the school day if it holds any of nine additives, starting in the 2026-2027 school year. The list covers potassium bromate, propylparaben, and seven artificial colors, among them Red No. 3 and Yellow No. 5. Parents may still bring those foods to their own children, and a teacher may hand them out with written permission from parents each semester. The limits do not reach concession stands at school events or vending machines, and they do not apply at a charter school or district with 5,500 students or fewer. The Utah House passed it 38-34 and it was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 403, which orders the Utah Department of Workforce Services to ask the federal government for permission to stop people from using food stamps to buy soft drinks. The act counts a sweetened fizzy drink as a soft drink. It leaves out drinks with milk in them and drinks that are more than half juice. The department had to file the request by July 1, 2025. If the request is granted, the state must act within six months. If it is refused, the state must file again within three months, and then once a year until it is granted. Nothing changes for shoppers unless the federal government agrees. The Utah House passed it 54-14 and it was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 477, which says that speaking at a school board meeting cannot by itself show the intent to annoy that the school trespass law requires. That holds so long as the comment follows the board's own rules on time, place, manner, and staying on topic. It also narrows what counts as school property for that crime. The law now reaches a school itself, and no longer reaches the offices or other property of a school district or charter school. The Utah House passed it 49-19 and it was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 78, which creates a state watchdog, called an ombudsman, to look into complaints about the groups that serve homeless people. The job sits inside the Office of Homeless Services. The ombudsman must run a website showing people how to complain. Each group must post the ombudsman's phone number and website where clients can see them. The ombudsman picks which complaints to take up. If a group has broken the law, the ombudsman must say so to the person who complained, to the office, and to a prosecutor. The Utah House passed it 43-28 and it was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 263, which makes the video of ballot processing a public record. Before this act, only a short list of officials could watch it. Election officers must now keep the paperwork that tracks where ballots have been for as long as they keep the ballots. They must also publish a count of the ballots they sent out and got back, broken down by how each one was sent and returned. County councils and other government bodies may look at electronic copies of ballots and envelopes. They must do so at the county clerk's office and may not take copies away. The Utah House passed it 47-23 and it was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for House Bill 100, which requires a school in the national lunch program to give free lunch to a student who already qualifies for a cheaper meal. The State Board of Education pays the school the difference. A school may not publicly single out a student who cannot pay. It must send notes about unpaid meal charges only to the student's parent. If lawmakers do not set aside enough money, the board splits what it has, and a school may ask parents to pay the rest. The Utah House passed it 47-24 and it was signed into law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 284, which tells the Utah Department of Health and Human Services to ask the federal government for permission to have Medicaid pay for doulas. A doula gives support, but not medical care, during pregnancy, birth, and the weeks after. If the federal government says yes, Medicaid must cover it. The department must also set training and sign-up rules for doulas who serve Medicaid patients. The Utah House passed it 55-16 and it was signed into law.
